extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history/literature; translators and editors of Schiller
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing readable, accurate historical works: use original sources, reconcile contradictions, and balance literary art with factual truth; also editorial guidance for translating and presenting Schiller's works to English readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive use of original sources and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indispensable to read them all to obtain that clear view of the whole subject to which the perusal of a part, however large, is always prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author lists numerous primary and secondary authorities (de Thou, Strada, Reyd, Grotius, Meteren, Burgundius, Meursius, Bentivoglio, Memoirs of Counsellor Hopper, correspondence of Viglius, records of trials, etc.) and notes the abundance (not paucity) of authorities. Read widely among contemporary documents to access material otherwise unavailable; consult compiled histories that abstract valuable foreign-language works when you cannot read the originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic truth combined with readability
rubrics_metrics.description: My aim in making this attempt will be more than attained if it should convince a portion of the reading public of the possibility of writing a history with historic truth without making a trial of patience to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to present accurate, truthful history while keeping prose engaging and not tedious; the objective is to avoid sacrificing readability for exhaustive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed introductory treatment to establish roots and actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer the reader delays on the introduction the more familiar he becomes with the actors in this history, and the scene in which they took a part, so much the more rapidly and unerringly shall I be able to lead him through the subsequent periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give careful attention to the introductory period (the 'root and source' of subsequent events). Even if the introduction seems minute or prolix, it prepares the reader and allows later narrative to proceed with greater clarity and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative synthesis: fill gaps and reconcile contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A closer acquaintance with my materials enabled me to discover defects previously unnoticed, long waste tracts to be filled up, apparent contradictions to be reconciled, and isolated facts to be brought into connection with the rest of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely compile more facts; seek keys to old facts, reconcile partial and contradictory narratives, connect isolated facts into a coherent whole, and prefer interpretive unity over mere accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity, soundness, and impartiality of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The admirable lucidity of style and soundness and impartiality of judgment displayed in his historical writings will not easily be surpassed, and will always recommend them as popular expositions of the periods of which they treat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clear expression, well-reasoned judgments, and impartiality; these qualities recommend a history to a broad readership and support its value as a popular exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance literary art with factual integrity (avoid romance)
rubrics_metrics.description: History can borrow from a cognate art without thereby, of necessity, becoming a romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the techniques of literary art (imagination, lively presentation) to enliven history, but maintain fidelity to facts and avoid turning history into fiction or romanticized embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and editorial practice for dramatic/poetic works
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached poems or dramas have been translated at various times since the first publication of the original works; ... this translation was too strictly literal for general readers. It has been carefully revised, and some portions have been entirely rewritten ... many passages not found in the printed edition are distinguished by brackets. On the other hand, Mr. Mellish omitted many passages which now form part of the printed drama, all of which are now added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For translated editions: revise overly literal translations to suit general readers, restore omitted passages when appropriate (mark them clearly, e.g., with brackets), respect the original arrangement when possible, and exercise restraint when revising earlier translators (revise 'with a sparing hand' in deference to their work). Provide editorial notes about source manuscripts and variations.
